1.pericope_label: Hezekiah began to reign when he was five and twenty years old, and he reigned nine and twenty years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah. And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done.

schools.summary: Delitzsch describes the position Hezekiah inherited and the two undertakings that followed — abolishing idolatry and restoring the lawful worship, then throwing off Assyrian subjection — and turns that into a point about the two histories, the older account spending its length on the revolt while this book gives the space to the cleansing; he also sets out why the date in the first month of the first year is disputed, since the Levites began on the first day and finished on the sixteenth while the king's summons came before any of it. Ellicott notes that the verse about doing right stands word for word with its counterpart.
Clarke refers his reader to his own note on the parallel rather than repeating himself.

themes: Hezekiah began to reign when he was five and twenty years old, and he reigned nine and twenty years in Jerusalem. And his mother’s name was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah.
And he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done.

3.pericope_label: He in the first year of his reign, in the first month, opened the doors of the house of the Lord, and repaired them. And he brought in the priests and the Levites, and gathered them together into the east street, And said unto them, Hear me, ye Levites, sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the Lord God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place.

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the month as Nisan, the first of the sacred year and not of the reign, reads the repairing as overlaying the doors with bronze or gold-leaf, and renders the verb of summoning as caused to come; Delitzsch places the gathering in the open space east of the temple rather than the inner court, insists on the order that the ministers sanctify themselves before the house, identifies the uncleanness as the abominations of idolatry, and grounds the whole summons in the devastation Ahaz had worked and the wrath that followed it.

Gill supplies the day from the later verse and describes the self-sanctifying concretely, as washing of bodies and garments so that no pollution should attend the service; he identifies the men summoned simply as those who officiated in the temple.

themes: He in the first year of his reign, in the first month, opened the doors of the house of the Lord, and repaired them.
And he brought in the priests and the Levites, and gathered them together into the east street,
And said unto them, Hear me, ye Levites, sanctify now yourselves, and sanctify the house of the Lord God of your fathers, and carry forth the filthiness out of the holy place.

6.pericope_label: For our fathers have trespassed, and done that which was evil in the eyes of the Lord our God, and have forsaken him, and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the Lord, and turned their backs. Also they have shut up the doors of the porch, and put out the lamps, and have not burned incense nor offered burnt offerings in the holy place unto the God of Israel. Wherefore the wrath of the Lord was upon Judah and Jerusalem, and he hath delivered them to trouble, to astonishment, and to hissing, as ye see with your eyes.

schools.summary: Ellicott sharpens the verb to dealt unfaithfully, explains the phrase about giving the neck as equivalent to turning it away, takes the description to be of Ahaz and his own generation, and itemises what was stopped — the porch that was the only entrance to the inner chambers, the lamps of the great golden stand, the incense of the golden altar — while explaining that the sanctuary here means the whole precinct and that the offerings on Ahaz's Syrian altar are counted as nothing because irregular; Delitzsch reads as ye see with your eyes as pointing to the defeats under Ahaz and the Syrian oppression.

Gill identifies the fathers as the immediate ancestors, calls their idolatry a trespass than which nothing is more provoking to God, says the shut porch left no entering the temple, and lists what the wrath looked like — Syrians, Israelites, Edomites and Philistines allowed to come up and distress them.
Wesley catches what the king does not say: he says they, not my father, because it became him as a son to be as tender as he could of his father's name.

outliers.claim: That the king's use of 'they' rather than 'my father' throughout the indictment is deliberate filial restraint — an unsparing charge about the deeds kept silent about the man.

themes: For our fathers have trespassed, and done that which was evil in the eyes of the Lord our God, and have forsaken him, and have turned away their faces from the habitation of the Lord, and turned their backs.
Also they have shut up the doors of the porch, and put out the lamps, and have not burned incense nor offered burnt offerings in the holy place unto the God of Israel.
Wherefore the wrath of the Lord was upon Judah and Jerusalem, and he hath delivered them to trouble, to astonishment, and to hissing, as ye see with your eyes.

9.pericope_label: For, lo, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this. Now it is in mine heart to make a covenant with the Lord God of Israel, that his fierce wrath may turn away from us. My sons, be not now negligent: for the Lord hath chosen you to stand before him, to serve him, and that ye should minister unto him, and burn incense.

schools.summary: Delitzsch explains that making a covenant here means renewing the existing one by restoring the lapsed worship, which is why the summons to the Levites follows at once, calls the address kindly language deliberately chosen, and notes that the verb forbidding negligence occurs nowhere else in this form and means letting a thing slip through carelessness rather than refusing it; Ellicott observes that the preposition is for rather than with and that the verb rendered turn away is literally return.

Gill identifies the fathers fallen by the sword as those killed by the kings of Syria and Israel, supplies the precedent for renewing a covenant from Asa and Jehoiada, and hears in the address my sons a father speaking to his people in the most tender and affectionate manner.

Clarke reaches back past Asa and Jehoiada to the covenant under which the whole people were constantly held and of which circumcision was the sign, stating its spirit in seven words: I will be your God, ye shall be my people.

themes: For, lo, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our sons and our daughters and our wives are in captivity for this.
Now it is in mine heart to make a covenant with the Lord God of Israel, that his fierce wrath may turn away from us.
My sons, be not now negligent: for the Lord hath chosen you to stand before him, to serve him, and that ye should minister unto him, and burn incense.

12.pericope_label: Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah: And of the sons of Elizaphan; Shimri, and Jeiel: and of the sons of Asaph; Zechariah, and Mattaniah: And of the sons of Heman; Jehiel, and Shimei: and of the sons of Jeduthun; Shemaiah, and Uzziel. And they gathered their brethren, and sanctified themselves, and came, according to the commandment of the king, by the words of the Lord, to cleanse the house of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott describes the same arrangement as seven pairs drawn from the three great Levitical houses and the remaining musical guilds, and points out that as heads of houses these men had the authority to summon their brethren, the families concerned being those resident in Jerusalem; Delitzsch attaches the words about the words of the Lord to the king's commandment rather than to the cleansing, so that the royal order is itself grounded in the written law, and gives the sequence — brethren gathered, all sanctified, then the work begun.
Gill walks the list of fourteen by family — two Kohathites, two Merarites, two Gershonites, two of Elizaphan's house, and two from each of the three musical families founded under David.

Wesley alone asks what cleansing a long-shut building involved, and answers domestically before theologically: the dust, cobwebs and rust it had contracted while closed, and then, far more, the idols and idolatrous altars.

themes: Then the Levites arose, Mahath the son of Amasai, and Joel the son of Azariah, of the sons of the Kohathites: and of the sons of Merari, Kish the son of Abdi, and Azariah the son of Jehalelel: and of the Gershonites; Joah the son of Zimmah, and Eden the son of Joah:
And of the sons of Elizaphan; Shimri, and Jeiel: and of the sons of Asaph; Zechariah, and Mattaniah:
And of the sons of Heman; Jehiel, and Shimei: and of the sons of Jeduthun; Shemaiah, and Uzziel.
And they gathered their brethren, and sanctified themselves, and came, according to the commandment of the king, by the words of the Lord, to cleanse the house of the Lord.

16.pericope_label: And the priests went into the inner part of the house of the Lord, to cleanse it, and brought out all the uncleanness that they found in the temple of the Lord into the court of the house of the Lord. And the Levites took it, to carry it out abroad into the brook Kidron. Now they began on the first day of the first month to sanctify, and on the eighth day of the month came they to the porch of the Lord: so they sanctified the house of the Lord in eight days; and in the sixteenth day of the first month they made an end. Then they went in to Hezekiah the king, and said, We have cleansed all the house of the Lord, and the altar of burnt offering, with all the vessels thereof, and the shewbread table, with all the vessels thereof. Moreover all the vessels, which king Ahaz in his reign did cast away in his transgression, have we prepared and sanctified, and, behold, they are before the altar of the Lord.

schools.summary: Delitzsch describes the relay by which priests carried uncleanness to the court and Levites beyond the city, gives the timetable from the first day to the sixteenth, and glosses the disputed verb as thrown away, that is, made worthy of rejection; Ellicott keeps the harder sense, matching the word to the term used elsewhere for casting off, names the pieces concerned, and notes that what the Levites say they have done to them is ordering aright, in a verb form occurring only here.

Gill takes the inner part for the holy place, which none but priests might enter, and raises on his own account the question how far in they went, allowing that in case of necessity others might enter the most holy place and supposing they may have done so here; on the vessels he refuses the literal sense of casting away, since gold and silver were too valuable to discard, and follows Kimchi and the Targum in reading it as removal to idolatrous use or as defilement.

Clarke sets out the division of labour most clearly — courts first and eight days spent on them, then the interior, with the priests carrying rubbish to the porch because the Levites had no right to enter, and eight days more, sixteen in all — and reports a Targum saying the polluted vessels were collected and hidden and others prepared to replace them.

debates.question: What did Ahaz actually do to the vessels?

positions.position: Not literally discarded them, being gold and silver; he removed them to idolatrous use, or defiled them.
Cast them off, in the strong sense the verb carries elsewhere.
Threw them away in the sense of making them worthy of rejection.
Polluted them, after which they were collected and hidden and replacements prepared.

themes: And the priests went into the inner part of the house of the Lord, to cleanse it, and brought out all the uncleanness that they found in the temple of the Lord into the court of the house of the Lord. And the Levites took it, to carry it out abroad into the brook Kidron.

Now they began on the first day of the first month to sanctify, and on the eighth day of the month came they to the porch of the Lord: so they sanctified the house of the Lord in eight days; and in the sixteenth day of the first month they made an end.

Then they went in to Hezekiah the king, and said, We have cleansed all the house of the Lord, and the altar of burnt offering, with all the vessels thereof, and the shewbread table, with all the vessels thereof.
Moreover all the vessels, which king Ahaz in his reign did cast away in his transgression, have we prepared and sanctified, and, behold, they are before the altar of the Lord.

20.pericope_label: Then Hezekiah the king rose early, and gathered the rulers of the city, and went up to the house of the Lord. And they brought seven bullocks, and seven rams, and seven lambs, and seven he goats, for a sin offering for the kingdom, and for the sanctuary, and for Judah. And he commanded the priests the sons of Aaron to offer them on the altar of the Lord. So they killed the bullocks, and the priests received the blood, and sprinkled it on the altar: likewise, when they had killed the rams, they sprinkled the blood upon the altar: they killed also the lambs, and they sprinkled the blood upon the altar. And they brought forth the he goats for the sin offering before the king and the congregation; and they laid their hands upon them: And the priests killed them, and they made reconciliation with their blood upon the altar, to make an atonement for all Israel: for the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains that only the rulers of the city were summoned because there was no time for a general call into the country, follows the ritual closely — blood caught in bowls and thrown toward the altar, the verb reserved for sacrificial slaughter, the three symmetrical clauses — and reads that repetition as the writer's anxiety to show the legitimate rite observed at every step; on the closing clause he takes all Israel to include the northern kingdom.

Gill reads the king's early rising as taking the first opportunity to worship and setting an example, and accounts for seven of each victim where the law required one by the multitude of transgressions and the length of time sacrifice had been neglected, distributing the purpose as the verse does between king, sanctuary and land.
Clarke reads the laying on of hands as confession, the offerers having forfeited their own lives and now presenting these animals to die in their place, a life taken for a life.

Henry says the king lost no time, and insists that lamenting and forsaking the sins of the last reign was not enough without a sin offering, drawing the conclusion that repentance and reformation obtain pardon only in and through Christ.

themes: Then Hezekiah the king rose early, and gathered the rulers of the city, and went up to the house of the Lord.

And they brought seven bullocks, and seven rams, and seven lambs, and seven he goats, for a sin offering for the kingdom, and for the sanctuary, and for Judah. And he commanded the priests the sons of Aaron to offer them on the altar of the Lord.

So they killed the bullocks, and the priests received the blood, and sprinkled it on the altar: likewise, when they had killed the rams, they sprinkled the blood upon the altar: they killed also the lambs, and they sprinkled the blood upon the altar.
And they brought forth the he goats for the sin offering before the king and the congregation; and they laid their hands upon them:

And the priests killed them, and they made reconciliation with their blood upon the altar, to make an atonement for all Israel: for the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.

25.pericope_label: And he set the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, with psalteries, and with harps, according to the commandment of David, and of Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet: for so was the commandment of the Lord by his prophets. And the Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. And Hezekiah commanded to offer the burnt offering upon the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song of the Lord began also with the trumpets, and with the instruments ordained by David king of Israel.

schools.summary: Delitzsch identifies the instruments as those David introduced into the public service, and explains the repeated clause about commanding the burnt offering as a connective, introducing the synchronism by which the song of the Lord began at the moment the sacrifice did.

Gill notes that the three principal instruments of worship had fallen into disuse under Ahaz, describes the burnt offering as wholly devoted to God in acknowledgement of his sovereignty and goodness, and identifies the instruments as David's in invention and direction.

Clarke stops longest here, observing that Moses appointed no instruments for worship and that the horns of the tabernacle served the function bells serve for us, that the instruments are David's innovation, and that the prophet Amos reproved those who devised music after David's manner — and then registers without resolving it that this chapter claims divine commandment for the arrangement.

outliers.claim: That the musical instruments of the temple were a Davidic innovation unknown to Moses, and that a prophet reproved music devised after David’s manner — a tension Clarke sets beside this chapter’s claim of divine commandment without resolving it.

themes: And he set the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, with psalteries, and with harps, according to the commandment of David, and of Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet: for so was the commandment of the Lord by his prophets.
And the Levites stood with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets.

And Hezekiah commanded to offer the burnt offering upon the altar. And when the burnt offering began, the song of the Lord began also with the trumpets, and with the instruments ordained by David king of Israel.

28.pericope_label: And all the congregation worshipped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded: and all this continued until the burnt offering was finished. And when they had made an end of offering, the king and all that were present with him bowed themselves, and worshipped. Moreover Hezekiah the king and the princes commanded the Levites to sing praise unto the Lord with the words of David, and of Asaph the seer. And they sang praises with gladness, and they bowed their heads and worshipped. Then Hezekiah answered and said, Now ye have consecrated yourselves unto the Lord, come near and bring sacrifices and thank offerings into the house of the Lord. And the congregation brought in sacrifices and thank offerings; and as many as were of a free heart burnt offerings.

schools.summary: Ellicott says these verses throw particular light on how the worship was conducted, renders the verbs as continuous, and explains the idiom by which the Hebrew says the song rather than the singers and uses a masculine participle of the feminine clarions because the instrument stands for its players, as an orchestra is said to have violins; Delitzsch records the kneeling at the close of the sacrificial act and explains the king's idiom of filling the hand to the Lord as being consecrated afresh to his service, which is the ground of the invitation that follows.

Gill describes the congregation bowing their heads as a token of divine adoration, notes that both offerings were meant when the offering is said to have ended, and identifies the psalms sung as compositions of David and of Asaph, passing on Jarchi's identification of the particular one.

themes: And all the congregation worshipped, and the singers sang, and the trumpeters sounded: and all this continued until the burnt offering was finished.
And when they had made an end of offering, the king and all that were present with him bowed themselves, and worshipped.

Moreover Hezekiah the king and the princes commanded the Levites to sing praise unto the Lord with the words of David, and of Asaph the seer. And they sang praises with gladness, and they bowed their heads and worshipped.

Then Hezekiah answered and said, Now ye have consecrated yourselves unto the Lord, come near and bring sacrifices and thank offerings into the house of the Lord. And the congregation brought in sacrifices and thank offerings; and as many as were of a free heart burnt offerings.

32.pericope_label: And the number of the burnt offerings, which the congregation brought, was threescore and ten bullocks, an hundred rams, and two hundred lambs: all these were for a burnt offering to the Lord. And the consecrated things were six hundred oxen and three thousand sheep. But the priests were too few, so that they could not flay all the burnt offerings: wherefore their brethren the Levites did help them, till the work was ended, and until the other priests had sanctified themselves: for the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests. And also the burnt offerings were in abundance, with the fat of the peace offerings, and the drink offerings for every burnt offering. So the service of the house of the Lord was set in order. And Hezekiah rejoiced, and all the people, that God had prepared the people: for the thing was done suddenly.

schools.summary: Delitzsch calls the spontaneous contribution very large, reports without softening the text's own reason for the Levites helping, that they were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests, and reads the closing joy as being over what God had prepared for the people rather than over God having made the people ready, explicitly rejecting that alternative; Ellicott adds a second reason for the Levites' help, that the available priests were fully occupied with the service of the altar itself.

Gill sorts the totals by who ate what, the burnt offerings leaving the offerers no portion and the consecrated things being peace offerings of which the owners had a share, then sets the numbers in proportion — much smaller than under David and Solomon, because the nation was poorer and because this was the oblation of two tribes rather than of all Israel — and enlarges on how much work each offering carried.
Clarke ends where the chapter does, with king and people rejoicing together at what God had brought about.

positions.position: Over what God had prepared FOR the people — the purified house and the restored worship.
More simply, delight at seeing things go so well, which boded good for what was coming.

themes: And the number of the burnt offerings, which the congregation brought, was threescore and ten bullocks, an hundred rams, and two hundred lambs: all these were for a burnt offering to the Lord.
